problem: The claim that TLS 1.3 dropped classical finite-field Diffie-Hellman is wrong. TLS 1.3 still supports ephemeral finite-field DH through the standardised ffdhe2048/3072/4096/6144/8192 groups; what it removed was static (non-ephemeral) DH and RSA key transport, not FFDHE itself.
fix: Real deployments prefer X25519 or the NIST P-256 curve for ECDHE. TLS 1.3 removed static DH and RSA key transport and keeps only ephemeral key exchange, ECDHE in practice and FFDHE with the standardised ffdhe groups.

problem: The symbol g is reused with a different meaning. Section 1 defines g as a primitive root of the full group mod p, but here g = h² mod p is a generator of the order-q subgroup only, so it is not a primitive root of the full group. A student may think both statements describe the same number.
fix: State it explicitly: in safe-prime mode a different symbol, say g_q = h² mod p, is a generator of the order-q subgroup; it has order q, not p−1, and it is not a primitive root of the full group.

problem: "It also removes the smooth part of p − 1 that Pohlig-Hellman would exploit" is loose: with p = 2q + 1 the only factors of p − 1 are 2 and q, so there is no long smooth part to remove.
fix: The subgroup order q is prime, so Pohlig-Hellman has no small factors to split along; the only small subgroup left in the full group, of order 2, sits outside the subgroup you work in.

problem: The two dashed messages 'K = Bᵃ = 2' (Alice to Bob) and 'K = Aᵇ = 2' (Bob to Alice) are drawn as network messages, which can suggest that K is transmitted. K is never sent.
fix: Label them as local computation, for example 'Alice computes K = Bᵃ = 2' and 'Bob computes K = Aᵇ = 2', or keep the dashed arrows but caption them 'not sent — computed locally'.
